summary: Discusses issues in giving the ECN field in the IP header meanings other than those in RFC 3168. It sets requirements so such alternative uses can coexist safely with routers that follow the original behavior. This is a Best Current Practice.

eli5.summary: Routers use two small flag bits to say the road is getting busy. If someone wants those flags to mean something else, this note explains how to do it without confusing everyone else.

questions: can the ecn field be redefined
what happens when an old router sees alternate ecn traffic
what is the ce codepoint in ecn
subtitle: The ground rules for anyone who wants the IP ECN bits to mean something other than what RFC 3168 says.

tldr.problem: Several proposals give the ECN field in the IP header meanings other than those in RFC 3168, but the Internet contains many routers that do not understand the new meanings.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists the issues any such proposal must address and offers three options for safe deployment: keep it out of the global Internet, verify that routers on the path understand it, or define it to coexist fairly with default ECN.
tldr.outcome: A specification of alternate ECN semantics must state how it handles these issues and must meet the coexistence requirements. The RFC was later updated by RFC 6040.

today: RFC 4774 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 124) and has not been obsoleted, but it was updated by RFC 6040.

sections.title: Why Alternate ECN Semantics Need Rules
sections.content:
RFC 3168, a Proposed Standard, defines the ECN field in the IP header and the meaning of its codepoints. RFC 4774 observes that end nodes could specify alternate semantics for that field, for example by using codepoints in the diffserv field of the IP header.

Several proposals exist. One suggests alternate semantics for real-time inelastic traffic in DiffServ networks, giving information about two levels of congestion along the path. Another research proposal, the Variable-structure congestion Control Protocol (VCP), uses the two ECN bits to signal low-load, high-load and overload. Others use ECN edge-to-edge between gateways at the edge of a network region, for example for pre-congestion notification for admission control.

The concern is deployment. There is a huge base of installed hosts and routers, some can be upgraded in software, some only with costly hardware, and some could suffer performance degradation ranging from trivial to catastrophic. So the document describes the technical issues and gives requirements for safe coexistence with the default ECN semantics, or with no ECN at all.
sections.eli5: Everyone already agrees what the two flags mean. Changing the meaning is like changing what a traffic light color means, so you need rules first.

sections.title: The Four Questions
sections.content:
The RFC frames the problem as four issues, where alternate-ECN traffic is traffic using alternate semantics for the ECN field, new routers understand those semantics and old routers do not or will not use them.

  1. How do routers know which ECN semantics apply to which packets, and is that signal robust and unambiguous?
  2. How does the possible presence of old routers affect the performance of the alternate-ECN connection?
  3. How does the presence of old routers affect the coexistence of alternate-ECN traffic with competing traffic?
  4. How well does the alternate-ECN traffic perform and coexist in a clean environment of new routers with unambiguous signalling?

Section 3 addresses the first, Section 4 the second and third, and Section 5 the fourth.
sections.eli5: Before changing the rules of the road, ask: how will drivers know, what if some roads still use the old signs, and will the new way be fair?

sections.title: Signalling the Alternate Semantics
sections.content:
The document assumes that a codepoint in the diffserv field signals alternate ECN semantics. The end host sets the codepoint. Routers that understand it interpret and set the ECN field accordingly, while old ECN-capable routers that do not understand it use the default semantics. The RFC does not exclude other methods, including out-of-band mechanisms, and says its considerations apply whichever method is used.

It notes that the default semantics from RFC 3168 apply regardless of the contents of any other field in the IP header, not just for best-effort traffic with the diffserv codepoint 000000.

There are two ways to use the diffserv field. One is to redefine an existing codepoint through approved IETF processes. The other is to define a new codepoint. The first raises the possibility that some routers along the path understand the codepoint but use default ECN semantics or no ECN, while others use the alternate semantics. One could also pair a codepoint for a per-hop behavior with default ECN and another for a similar behavior with alternate ECN, or use a codepoint for best-effort queueing with alternate ECN. A detailed discussion is out of scope.
sections.eli5: The sender puts a special sticker on the packet that says "read my flags the new way". Routers that know the sticker follow it. Routers that do not just use the old way.

sections.title: Incremental Deployment and Three Options
sections.content:
The danger is old routers. A non-ECN old router that is congested drops packets and expects senders to slow down. An old router that follows RFC 3168 may see an ECT codepoint on an alternate-ECN packet and set the Congestion Experienced (CE) codepoint instead of dropping. If the alternate-ECN sender ignores that mark, traffic at the router grows, marking and dropping rise further, and the alternate-ECN traffic crowds out competing flows.

The RFC sees three ways to avoid unfair competition.

  • Option 1: unsafe for the global Internet. The traffic is understood as suitable only for enclosed environments, which would keep it from crossing old routers outside. The RFC does not say whether a mechanism to enforce this would be required, nor whether the IETF would accept it for standardization.
  • Option 2: verify the path. The traffic carries a mechanism proving every router understands and agrees to the alternate semantics. An example is an IP option field that each agreeing router decrements, similar to Quick-Start. The catch is that most routers are optimized for packets with no options, so a new option may seriously hurt performance. The mechanism should also cope with multi-path routing and path changes, perhaps with periodic monitoring.
  • Option 3: coexist safely. The semantics are defined so the traffic behaves fairly even across old routers. A sender must respond to a CE packet (ECN codepoint 11) with a conformant congestion control response, and should also respond appropriately to dropped packets.
sections.eli5: You can keep the new rules inside a private playground, check that every road has the new signs, or invent new rules that still work with the old signs.

sections.title: Coexistence Requirements
sections.content:
RFC 3168 requires that on receipt of a single CE packet, end-system congestion control be essentially the same as the response to a single dropped packet. For ECN-capable TCP, the source halves its congestion window for any window containing a drop or an ECN indication. The conformant mechanisms the RFC lists are TCP and TCP-like congestion control (including SCTP and DCCP with CCID-2) and TCP-Friendly Rate Control (TFRC), including DCCP using CCID-3.

For compatibility with routers using default ECN, two requirements apply. First, a packet marked 11 in the network must not have that marking changed on its way to the receiver unless it is dropped, so congestion signals reach the receiver. Second, end nodes must respond to 11-marked packets in a way that is friendly to flows using IETF-conformant congestion control, so they do not bully competing traffic.

For compatibility with end nodes using default ECN, which matters if a codepoint is redefined and old-source traffic crosses a new router, a packet that could be using default semantics and is marked 00 must not be changed to 01, 10 or 11. A packet marked 01 should not be changed to 10, nor 10 to 01, to avoid interfering with the ECN nonce. These extra rules are unnecessary if the router knows from the diffserv codepoint that the sender uses alternate semantics.

The RFC also mentions another response considered in RFC 3714 but not standardized: terminating a connection for a period if its long-term rate exceeds that of a TCP connection seeing the same drop or marking rates. That would need defined time constants and attention to packet size.
sections.eli5: If a router shouts "slow down" with the old signal, the new traffic must really slow down, and nobody may secretly change one signal into another.

sections.title: Evaluating the Alternate Semantics
sections.content:
Section 5 covers a clean environment where all routers understand the alternate semantics.

  • Verifying feedback. A receiver may have an incentive to lie about congestion. Default ECN uses two ECN-Capable codepoints, ECT(0) and ECT(1), so a sender can check receiver reports as described in RFC 3540. Alternate semantics without two such codepoints lose that ability and may need other mechanisms, such as policers in routers.
  • Coexistence. Best-effort alternate-ECN traffic must compete fairly with TCP and other traffic per RFC 2914. For diffserv traffic, requirements come from the guidelines for that class and from the codepoint's own specification.
  • Edge-to-edge semantics. These must not conflict with a connection using other ECN semantics end-to-end, either by being kept off such connections or by being defined not to conflict.
  • Encapsulated packets. Proposals must explicitly consider interaction with IP tunnels, including IPsec and IP in IP, which RFC 3168 discusses extensively.
  • General merits. The RFC leaves requirements for the general evaluation out of scope.
sections.eli5: Even with perfect new signs everywhere, someone could cheat by lying about what they saw, and tunnels might hide the signs. Anyone proposing a change has to think about those too.

sections.title: Security and Conclusions
sections.content:
The document proposes no new mechanisms for the Internet protocol, so it states that it introduces no new security considerations. Its feedback-verification discussion is about receivers lying and is covered under the evaluation of alternate semantics.

The conclusions are short but binding on proposers. Specifications of alternate ECN semantics must clearly state how they address the issues in Section 2, and they must meet the coexistence requirements in Section 5.2.
sections.eli5: This note does not add any new locks or keys. It only tells people proposing new ECN meanings what they must explain and promise.

viz.caption: WHAT AN OLD ROUTER DOES (RFC 4774, FIGURE 1)
THE THREE OPTIONS FOR SAFE DEPLOYMENT

items.title: Option 1
items.text: Alternate ECN is understood as unsafe for the global Internet.

items.title: Option 2
items.text: A mechanism verifies that all routers on the path agree to the semantics.

items.title: Option 3
items.text: The semantics are defined to coexist fairly with old routers.
